rationale: I'm adding sample location (stool / terminal ileum / rectum) as one-hot features. Biopsy and stool communities differ a lot, and the published baselines also differ by site (0.71 for stool, 0.85 for biopsies). With location as a feature, the random forest can learn separate disease signatures for each site instead of treating site differences as noise. On the other stool-only studies the location columns are constant, so this change can't hurt transfer there. I haven't run this here, so I don't have a Dev score for it yet.

I'm adding four alpha-diversity features computed from the raw counts: OTU-level Shannon, Simpson, genus-level Shannon, and Hurlbert rarefied richness at 1000 reads. Crohn's dysbiosis is consistently linked to lower diversity. That is a signal spread across the whole community, and a random forest splitting on single genus abundances can only approximate it. Rarefied richness and Shannon are much less sensitive to sequencing depth than raw richness, so these features should also carry over to the other stool studies. I haven't run this, so I don't have a Dev score for it yet.

I'm replacing the single genus table with one built from the full taxonomic lineage at every level from phylum to genus. In the current version every unclassified genus (`g__`) from every family is merged into one feature, which is meaningless. Higher levels also matter for IBD: family-level shifts like gain of Enterobacteriaceae and Fusobacteriaceae, and loss of the Ruminococcaceae and Lachnospiraceae families, are among its most consistent signals. Many 16S reads are only classified down to family, so those levels hold signal the genus table drops, and taxon names at these levels match across studies, which should help transfer. I haven't run this, so I don't have a Dev score for it yet.

I'm adding an L2-regularized logistic regression on CLR-transformed genera, filtered to genera present in at least 10% of samples, and averaging its probabilities with the existing random forest. Crohn's dysbiosis is a broad, roughly log-linear shift in many taxa at once (Faecalibacterium and Roseburia down, Enterobacteriaceae and Fusobacterium up), which a compositional linear model captures well and should carry over to other studies, while the forest captures nonlinear and location-specific effects. The regularization strength C is chosen by inner grouped CV on the training fold, using `ctx["groups_train"]`. I haven't run this, so I don't have a Dev score for it yet.

I'm filtering out rare genera inside each training fold, keeping only those detected (nonzero) in at least 10% of training samples, before fitting the random forest. Round 3 showed that adding many sparse, redundant features hurts this forest (0.765). Rare genera are mostly noise: they are often study-specific and depend on sequencing depth, yet the sqrt feature sampling still picks them at many splits. Dropping them should make the forest split on the abundant core taxa that carry the Crohn's dysbiosis signal and that transfer across studies. I haven't run this, so I don't have a Dev score for it yet.

Each subject contributes several samples (stool plus biopsies), so a fully grown forest (min_samples_leaf=1) can learn individual subjects' communities rather than the Crohn's dysbiosis pattern, and that won't carry over to new subjects or studies. I'm choosing min_samples_leaf from {1, 3, 8} using inner grouped CV on the training fold (grouped by `ctx["groups_train"]`), then refitting with more trees (1000) to lower variance. Features are unchanged. I haven't run this, so I don't have a Dev score for it yet.

At the moment every OTU with an empty genus (`g__`) is pooled into one feature. That mixes unclassified Enterobacteriaceae, which rise in Crohn's, with unclassified Ruminococcaceae and Lachnospiraceae, which fall, so their signals largely cancel. I'm labelling each such OTU by its deepest named rank instead (e.g. `f__Enterobacteriaceae|unclassified`). This keeps the compact genus-level table and avoids round 3's redundant multi-level features, while recovering family-level dysbiosis signal that also carries over to other studies.

Stool and biopsy communities have very different baseline genus abundances. A single split threshold such as "Faecalibacterium < 2%" therefore means different things at each site, and the forest has to spend its depth learning a separate threshold per location. I'm replacing each genus abundance with its mid-rank percentile among training samples from the same location. This location-wise normalization puts all three sites on one scale, so splits on Crohn's dysbiosis are shared across stool, terminal-ileum and rectal samples. The location one-hot features are kept.

I'm adding Gevers' microbial dysbiosis index (MDI) as one feature. It is the log ratio of the taxa that rise in Crohn's (Enterobacteriaceae, Pasteurellaceae, Veillonellaceae, Fusobacteriaceae) to those that fall (Erysipelotrichales, Bacteroidales, Clostridiales). This index was defined on this RISK cohort. It compresses a community-wide shift into one value that a forest splitting on single genera can only approximate, and because it uses family and order names it should carry over to the other IBD stool studies. Like the genus columns, it goes through the per-location percentile normalization.

I'm replacing the random forest with an ExtraTrees classifier and raising the tree count from 500 to 1000; features and preprocessing stay the same. The per-location percentile features already sit on a common 0–1 scale, so random split thresholds work well on them. Each subject contributes several samples, and the extra randomization should stop trees from fitting thresholds to one subject's community, which should help the model carry over to new subjects and to the other stool studies.

I'm changing the ExtraTrees `max_features` from `sqrt` to 0.15, so each split looks at about 15% of the genera instead of about 6%. The Crohn's signal sits in a small core of dysbiosis taxa (e.g. Faecalibacterium/Roseburia loss and Enterobacteriaceae/Fusobacterium/Veillonellaceae gain), while most of the hundreds of genus columns are sparse noise. Round 5 suggests that noise can't simply be filtered out, but with `sqrt` sampling many splits never see a core taxon. ExtraTrees' random thresholds keep the trees diverse even with more candidates per split. I haven't run this, so I don't have a Dev score for it yet.

Each training sample will be weighted by 1/(number of samples its subject contributes), using `ctx["groups_train"]`. Subjects with stool plus two biopsies currently count three times as much as single-sample subjects. Equal weight per subject should push the trees toward the Crohn's dysbiosis pattern shared across many subjects, rather than the particular communities of the most heavily sampled ones. That should carry over better to new subjects and to the other stool studies.

Sequencing depth varies a lot, so a genus seen at 1–2 reads in a deep sample would simply be absent from a shallow one. These depth-driven zeros and near-zeros currently get very different per-location percentiles. I'm zeroing any genus whose relative abundance falls below a common detection limit, 1/(10th-percentile depth, label-free, capped at 1e-3). Presence/absence then means the same thing in every sample, and the forest should split on real abundance differences rather than on sampling noise, which should also carry over to studies with other depths. Not run yet, so no Dev score.

The per-location percentile transform is currently computed in `fit_predict` against the training samples only. I'm moving it into `featurize` and computing each sample's genus percentiles against all samples from the same study and sample location (label-free; falls back to location-wide, then global, when a group has fewer than 20 samples). Within Gevers this should behave much like the current per-location reference. The real gain should be transfer: the other IBD stool studies would each be ranked against their own samples, which cancels study-specific differences in depth, sequencing region and OTU calling (the Gibbons-style per-study percentile normalization), instead of being placed on the Gevers training distribution. This is untested, so I have no Dev score for it yet; on Dev I expect a score close to 0.845 rather than a clear gain.

I'm lowering ExtraTrees `max_features` from `sqrt` (about 17 genera per split) to `log2` (about 8), and raising the tree count to 2000 so the extra randomness is averaged out. So far every step toward more randomization has helped: switching from RF to ExtraTrees gained about 0.02, and round 11's move to more candidates per split lost about 0.013. That fits a Crohn's signal spread across many genera, which is better captured by an average of many weakly correlated trees than by trees that keep picking the same strongest taxa and fitting individual subjects. This is untested, so I have no Dev score for it yet.

I'm training a second ExtraTrees model on family-level abundances, using the same per-location percentile normalization and location one-hot features, and averaging its probabilities with the genus-level model. The family table captures broad Crohn's dysbiosis shifts (Enterobacteriaceae and Fusobacteriaceae up, Ruminococcaceae and Lachnospiraceae down) and is less affected by how each study classifies genera, which should help on the other IBD studies. Round 3 put every taxonomic level into one forest and diluted the genus features; a separate forest per level avoids that.

Following Gibbons et al.'s case-control percentile normalization, each genus will now be converted to its mid-rank percentile among the training **non-IBD controls** of the same location, instead of among all training samples there. Crohn's prevalence differs between stool and biopsy sites. Ranking against all samples mixes disease into each site's reference, while ranking against healthy controls lines the sites up on the same "healthy baseline" scale, so a shared split like "below the 10th healthy percentile of Faecalibacterium" means the same thing at every site. Within a site this only rescales the values, so any change in score comes from better alignment across sites. I haven't run it, so there is no Dev score yet.

Crohn's disease looks different at each site. In ileal biopsies it shows mostly as mucosa-associated Enterobacteriaceae/Fusobacteria bloom, while in stool it shows as broad loss of Clostridiales. The pooled ExtraTrees model rarely splits on the location columns under `sqrt` sampling, so it mostly learns signatures shared across sites. I'm averaging its probabilities with a per-location ExtraTrees model trained only on training samples from the same site (when that site has enough samples), so site-specific signals are captured too. The pooled model stays in the average because it gives cross-site calibration and more data for the shared signal. Not run yet, so no Dev score.

I'm replacing the single ExtraTrees fit with a subject-level bagged ensemble: 25 ExtraTrees models of 80 trees each, each trained on a random two-thirds of training subjects. Plain ExtraTrees shows every tree all of every subject's stool and biopsy samples, so trees can learn individual subjects. Leaving out whole subjects per bag should make the trees less correlated and favour the Crohn's dysbiosis pattern shared across subjects, which should carry over better to new subjects and studies. I haven't run this, so there is no Dev score yet.

This adds a "healthy-reference" dysbiosis score, the beta-diversity measure from Lloyd-Price 2019: the median Bray-Curtis distance from each sample to the training non-IBD controls at the same site, plus a contrast feature, its median distance to controls minus its median distance to Crohn's samples. Crohn's dysbiosis is a whole-community move away from the healthy state, and trees splitting on one genus at a time can only approximate that. To avoid leakage, training-sample scores are computed out-of-fold with inner grouped CV on `ctx["groups_train"]`. I haven't run this, so there is no Dev score for it yet.
